strengths: Using stable diffusion as a distillation approach is interesting.
The paper is well-written, with most figures well-designed, illustrated, and easy to follow.
Modules such as gradient descent based prompt fitting are proposed to solve the inconsistency problem of diffusion model generation in video streaming transmission.
Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in LPIPS, compression ratio.
The real-time issues are well covered in the supplementary material.
Novel application of GAN AI for video streaming: By leveraging Stable Diffusion for video generation through prompts, Promptus introduces a novel approach to reducing video bandwidth requirements.
The gradient descent-based prompt fitting framework ensures pixel-level alignment, maintaining visual consistency with original frames, which is challenging for generative models.
The low-rank decomposition approach allows Promptus to adjust bitrate based on network conditions, enhancing usability in fluctuating bandwidth situation.
Temporal smoothing regularization reduces the need to transmit prompts for every frame, significantly cutting down bandwidth usage.
Promptus shows a marked improvement in bandwidth efficiency, achieving a fourfold reduction over H.265 while maintaining perceptual quality, especially in complex or high-frequency video content.

Clear setting. Reducing video bitrate is a practical and important problem, as video traffic can be quite expensive for content providers. This paper offers a revolutionary new perspective by representing videos with prompts and employing generative models for video reconstruction.

Well motivation. The main ideas and tricks can be easily understood. Many concerns at first glance are addressed in the following sections. The paper systematically discusses the challenges of prompt streaming, such as bitrate control, inter-frame compression, and real-time playback, and presents a comprehensive solution.
Simple yet effective, making it easy to follow. In the gradient descent framework, there appear to be many potential improvements for further work.
Novel in the sense of reforming the paradigm of traditional video streaming system by transmitting prompt streaming instead of video streaming.
Ensure pixel alignment in this kind of paradigm based on generative model is inspiring.
The workflow of the proposed method is well presented. The effectiveness of components is well discussed.
The authors openly discuss limitations of using prompts for video streaming system.
Promptus provides a new communication paradigm, using only prompts to stream a video.
The paper is easy to understand well and clearly written.

The effect at low bitrates is significantly improved. Compared with VAE and H.265, Promptus's perceptual quality is improved by 0.139 and 0.118 (in LPIPS), respectively, and the proportion of severely distorted frames is reduced by 89.3% and 91.7%, respectively.
weaknesses: My major concern is whether there are severe flicker issues or temporal over-smoothing in the decoded video, as the authors did not submit any video as a supplementary file. Considering that the rebuttal can only show images, I suggest the authors present an x-t slice, as used in [1], for a highly dynamic video. The x-t slice would provide a better visual understanding on the temporal consistency.

Could the authors justify why it is necessary to use stable diffusion as the intermediate medium for video compression? Why not directly use CLIP or the SD decoder to distill the frames? Is it because CLIP is not powerful enough?

The VAE could introduce significant color tone-mapping issues and spatial blurriness. Did the authors encounter similar issues on a large scale? I can see severe color issues in Figure 10, particularly in the boy's eye and background. Consequently, I am also concerned about some analyses in Section 4.4. In my understanding, the performance drop on the Animerun dataset occurs because those frames are edge cases for SD/VAE, which is why there are numerous color mapping issues.

Since the VAE and diffusion models are fixed, how do the authors ensure that the frames being represented and compressed fall within the diffusion model's domain of knowledge? Additionally, is the main source of encoding performance derived from CLIP/VAE or the U-Net? I did not see a related discussion on this matter.
The qualitative result comparisons are insufficient and do not convincingly demonstrate the proposed method's promise.

The method requires 8952 MB of memory to run, which is much higher than most existing methods, limiting practical applicability on devices with limited video memory such as mobile phones; the paper does not explore trade‑offs between memory usage and compression performance.

The paper does not adequately explore failure modes of the diffusion model (e.g., “multiple fingers”, “words cannot express” problems) and lacks experiments demonstrating how the proposed method performs on these unique diffusion model issues.

It is unclear whether Promptus can effectively transmit videos at resolutions not seen during SD‑Turbo or LCM training; the paper lacks a detailed investigation of the impact of resolution on performance and does not provide systematic resolution‑variation experiments.

The specific diffusion model version used is not stated in the main text; the paper also omits detailed breakdowns of encoding/decoding time and memory overhead, making it difficult to assess practical viability compared to existing codecs.

Unclear how the model handles abrupt scene cuts within videos; prompts optimized for one scene may not generalize to an entirely different visual context, potentially misrepresenting scene transitions.

As bitrate decreases, Promptus reduces the descriptive capacity of prompts; it is unclear how the model maintains accurate content representation at lower bitrates and why this simplification does not lead to misalignments in generated frames.
The paper predominantly relies on LPIPS as the primary evaluation metric; incorporating additional metrics such as SSIM or VMAF would provide a more holistic assessment of visual quality.
The paper lacks direct comparisons with the computational complexity and runtime of other state‑of‑the‑art benchmarks.
Experimental results compare Promptus only with H.265 and a VAE model, omitting comparisons with other recent SOTA video compression and generation benchmarks.
Considering that random packet loss occurs in network transmission, how would this influence the performance of Promptus? Would incomplete prompts severely degrade the quality of the generated video?
The authors do not explicitly compare Promptus with semantic communication; it is unclear whether Promptus is an instance of semantic communication or a potential alternative.
The paper should thoroughly clarify the fundamental differences between prompt inversion and video encoding/decoding; the authors do not provide further explanation beyond a brief mention.
Scalability concerns: the overhead of inversion from video to prompts may increase on a video platform with billions of users; the paper does not discuss how this cost scales.
Figures 8, 9, and 10 do not include a comparison of the results with representative methods from recent SOTA neural video compression works; the significance of the comparison with VAE is unclear.
PSNR and SSIM should still be considered alongside LPIPS.
More comparisons of subjective results at different bitrates are needed to highlight advantages on pixel alignment.
The increase in model parameters due to incorporating Stable Diffusion should be discussed, and more details on the training process should be provided.
Experiments and evaluation are not sufficient enough.
Only the decoding time is listed in the appendix, but not the encoding time.
Generated video sequences are not open‑sourced or shown frame‑by‑frame to prove stability of generation.
More subjective comparison results are needed to prove the advantages of Promptus at low bitrates.
The paper only mentions interpolation of prompt; it should be compared with interpolation in the pixel domain regarding generation performance and complexity.
There is a lack of comparison with other specific state‑of‑the‑art video compression methods (e.g., [1][2]).

The diffusion‑based video compression method shows several limitations, such as relatively large delay and complexity because prompts need to be inserted into intermediate frames, requiring subsequent frames before playback; it is also currently limited to low‑bitrate video streaming scenarios.
